newsitem.title: MEXICO: Joyous Mexicans celebrate opposition victory.
newsitem.headline: Joyous Mexicans celebrate opposition victory.

text.p: Thousands of people filled the Mexican capital's main square early on Monday to celebrate the victory of left-wing opposition leader Cuauhtemoc Cardenas in the city's first election for mayor.
They greeted the 63-year-old Cardenas with chants of "Viva Cuauhtemoc" when he appeared in the Zocalo square, where Aztec kings met Spanish conquerer Hernan Cortez in the 16th Century.
"Brothers and sisters, this is the people's victory, all Mexicans won," a smiling Cardenas told the crowd.
Supporters of Cardenas' left-leaning Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) waved giant yellow flags emblazoned with the party's symbol of an Aztec sun.
On Mexico City's Reforma avenue, PRD supporters honked their horns and waved the party's banner.
"Now it is up to us to organise ourselves and run this city well to solve its problems," Cardenas told residents of an 18-million-strong city wracked by pollution and crime.
Following his speech, the crowd raised their arms in a sea of V-for-victory signs used by Cardenas since he narrowly lost the 1988 presidential race, a defeat he attributed to fraud.
Holding their arms aloft, the crowd sang Mexico's national anthem. Some wept with joy.
"I'm so happy, it's something that we have been waiting a long time for," said Arturo Cruz, 27, draped in a yellow flag.

It was the first time the inhabitants of Mexico City have been allowed to choose their mayor. For 68 years, the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party has appointed the mayor, an institution known as the "dedazo," literally the pointing of a finger by the president.
"This is the people's dedazo," said 40-year-old Cardenas supporter Marcos Morales, holding up an ink-stained thumb to show he had voted earlier in the day.
Cardenas, the son of a popular former president in the 1930s, has vowed to make fighting crime and corruption his top priorities in governing the city.
A former PRI state governor who left the party in disgust in the 1980s, he is also widely expected to use the post as a platform for his third presidential bid in 2000.
Although his power over the city budget is restricted, the post is considered the second most important elected position in the country, after the president himself.
